extracted.intended_audience: fanfiction authors (users of Archive of Our Own / AO3) who want guidance on tagging their works
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for choosing and using AO3 freeform/additional tags: what types of tags to add, how many to use, content-warning etiquette, and platform-specific behaviors (e.g., hiding tags, tag wrangling).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory archive tags
rubrics_metrics.description: You must choose a fandom, a rating, and an archive warning from the available options (or explicitly choose not to use those options).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mandatory tags have detailed explanation boxes on AO3. They are required metadata separate from freeform tags and should be used correctly (or indicate you chose not to use them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of freeform/additional tags (optional but recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freeform tags are optional but give readers additional info about your fic and help readers find or avoid your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are entirely free to choose any keywords or phrases (including misspellings or new coinages). Freeform tags can attract readers who like particular tropes or help a former reader find a story without remembering title/author. They also let readers who dislike certain content avoid it. AO3 allows authors to hide freeform tags by default for logged-in users, so authors can tag without forcing spoilers on everyone.

rubrics_metrics.name: AO3 tag wrangling / canonicalization
rubrics_metrics.description: If you create a new freeform tag, AO3 tag-wrangling staff may check it and decide whether it fits into a more common category or should stand alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can introduce new tags, but they may be merged or mapped to canonical tags by AO3 volunteers or staff to keep discoverability consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag visibility / spoiler concern
rubrics_metrics.description: AO3 offers the option to hide freeform tags as a default for logged-in users, so tags can be present without exposing spoilers to all readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can rely on this feature to warn/readers without spoiling plot points; readers control whether to view tags. Consider readers' preferences: some avoid spoilers and others prefer knowing tropes beforehand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended number of tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an appropriate number of freeform tags to balance informativeness and clutter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested: 3–7 tags for shorter stories (<5k words). For longer stories, readers often want more detail—up to ~20 tags is acceptable. More than that tends to look cluttered and distracting. This is subjective guidance based on reader behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tags to indicate fixed format, length, or stylistic form of the fic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common format tags include: (Double/Triple) Drabble; Epistolary; Ficlet (Collection); Imagine; Novel/Novella; (Short) One Shot; Poetry; POV First Person; Self-Insert; Screenplay/Script Format; Songfic; Stand Alone; Vignette. These help set expectations about structure and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Tag broad genre descriptors so readers know the overall tone or category of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fanfic genre examples: Action/Adventure; Angst; Badfic; Character Study; Crack; Dark(-fic); Fluff; Friendship; Humor; Horror; Kidfic; Romance; RPF/RPS; Porn Without Plot/Plot What Plot. Genre can be messy/overlapping; use alongside other tags for specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship-to-canon tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate how your story relates to the original source material (canon): whether it follows, diverges from, or reimagines it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common tags: Alternate Timeline; Alternate Universe; Alternate Universe: X (e.g., werewolves); Backstory; Canon-compliant; Canon-divergent; Crossover; Fix-It; Fusion; Missing Scene; Post-Canon; Pre-Canon/Pre-Series; Reboot. These are especially useful in fanfic where deviations from source matter to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fandom-specific tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Use tags that identify which portion/era/element of a broad fandom your story focuses on, or fandom-specific events/conventions/tropes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in Harry Potter fandom you might tag 'Marauders' Era' or 'The Golden Trio Era'. Also include tags for fandom-specific events like Big Bangs/Reverse Big Bangs or fandom-exclusive tropes. These are helpful when a fandom covers many distinct settings/timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common fanfic trope tags
rubrics_metrics.description: Tag recognizable recurring tropes that signal story beats or relationship dynamics to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: Domestic; Everyone is alive; Fuck or Die; Getting together; Hurt/Comfort; Pining; Sex Pollen; Slow Burn; Soulmates; Time Travel; UST; Whump. These are more specific than genre and often drive reader interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory AO3 content warnings (the "big four")
rubrics_metrics.description: AO3 requires selecting an archive warning for underage sexual content, non-consensual/rape, graphic depictions of violence, and character death (the site’s 'big four'), or explicitly indicating you chose not to use them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These mandatory warnings must be used appropriately. They appear as required metadata separate from freeform tags and are crucial for reader safety and site policy compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optional additional content warnings and etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are not required to add further content warnings beyond the mandatory ones, but many fandoms consider it good etiquette to tag 'squicky' or triggering topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits of extra content warnings: (1) frames problematic behavior as problematic (signals author awareness), (2) helps readers avoid content they dislike, and (3) helps readers intentionally searching for dark/difficult topics find them. Common additional warnings: (Past/Implied) (Child/Emotional) Abuse; Age Difference; Alcohol/Drugs; Body Horror; Coercion/Jealousy/Manipulation; (Very) Dubious Consent; Gore; Kinks; Mental Health Issues (Eating Disorders, PTSD, Depression etc.); Pregnancy/Abortion/Miscarriage; (Internalized) Racism/Homophobia/Misogyny; Explicit Sexual Content; Terminal Illness; Torture; Suicide/Suicidal Thoughts. There is a more complete list linked from the post.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tagging as community etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Tagging problematic or squicky content has become a widespread fandom etiquette and is expected by many readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond site policy, consider community norms—tagging helps younger audiences and signals author responsibility. Failure to tag sensitive content can harm readers and hurt discoverability among those who would otherwise enjoy the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding tag clutter and maintaining clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep tags informative rather than creating huge, unreadable walls of tags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large numbers of tags often aren’t read in detail by most readers; aim for clarity and prioritise the most relevant tags. Excessive tags can look cluttered and distracting; be selective especially on shorter works.
